triage.name: Kidney Stones
triage.reason: Acute flank pain with hematuria; classic emergency and urology case with clear imaging and management decisions.

demographics: More common in men than women overall, though the gap has narrowed in recent decades
More common in the southeastern United States and other hot, dry climates
Higher rates in non-Hispanic white individuals and in some Middle Eastern and Asian populations
Recurrence is common; many patients have had a prior stone

risk_factors.text: Low fluid intake or chronic dehydration
High dietary sodium, animal protein, or oxalate
Hot climate or occupational heat exposure
Medullary sponge kidney or other anatomic urinary tract abnormality
Inflammatory bowel disease or bowel resection

family_history: Kidney stones in a parent or sibling
social_history: Occupational heat exposure or outdoor work
exposures: High dietary oxalate (spinach, rhubarb, nuts, chocolate)
Excess vitamin C or vitamin D supplementation

chief_complaints.text: The pain comes in waves and goes down to my groin
I can't get comfortable no matter what I do

hpi.onset: Sudden, often waking the patient from sleep or starting at rest; reaches full intensity within minutes to an hour
hpi.duration: Hours to days; pain may be intermittent as the stone moves
hpi.progression: Severe waxing and waning pain that comes in waves; may localize lower as the stone travels down the ureter; can become constant and dull if the stone obstructs and causes hydronephrosis
hpi.location: Flank or costovertebral angle, radiating downward and forward
hpi.radiation: From the flank to the lower abdomen, groin, and sometimes the genitalia or inner thigh
hpi.quality: Severe cramping or colicky, often described as the worst pain ever
hpi.timing: Paroxysmal; each wave lasts 20–60 minutes, with pain-free or less painful intervals early on
aggravating: Any attempt to find a comfortable position
relieving: Nothing reliably; patients often pace or writhe
Narcotic or NSAID analgesia in the emergency department

associated_symptoms.text: Blood in the urine (visible or microscopic)
Restlessness and inability to sit still

pertinent_negatives: Pain that is maximal and constant in the right lower quadrant
Pain that improves with lying still

positives.text: Feeling restless and unable to get comfortable
Feeling warm or sweaty from the pain

negatives: Pain localized to the right lower quadrant

atypical.how_it_differs: Pain may be milder or blunted, and presentation can be confused with musculoskeletal back pain or diverticulitis; fever may be absent even with obstruction.
Flank pain may be attributed to pregnancy-related discomfort; hydronephrosis of pregnancy can make imaging interpretation harder, and urinary stasis increases infection risk.
Young children may present with vague abdominal pain, vomiting, or irritability rather than a clear flank pain story.
Patients with chronic kidney disease may have less pain and are at higher risk for obstruction-related acute kidney injury; stone burden may be larger at presentation.
Higher risk of infection and emphysematous pyelonephritis; may present with sepsis rather than classic colic.
Higher stone recurrence and more difficult imaging; pain may be attributed to other causes.

general.mild: Restless but comfortable between pain waves; able to sit and talk
general.moderate: Writhing or pacing, unable to find a comfortable position, diaphoretic
general.severe: Marked restlessness, pale and diaphoretic, vomiting, in obvious distress
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic or confused, hypotensive, signs of sepsis or obstructive pyelonephritis

findings.maneuver: Percuss or gently press over the costovertebral angle on the symptomatic side
findings.finding: Costovertebral angle tenderness on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Palpate the flank and upper abdomen on the affected side

findings.finding: Mild, poorly localized abdominal tenderness; no focal right lower quadrant tenderness

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen and assess for guarding or rigidity
findings.finding: No guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness

findings.maneuver: Palpate the midline abdomen for a pulsatile mass
Ask the patient to cough or gently shake the bed
findings.finding: No pain with jarring beyond the flank

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature and assess for systemic signs

findings.finding: No tenderness on the unaffected side

labs.caveat: Hematuria is present in most but not all patients; a negative dipstick does not exclude a stone.
Sterile pyuria can occur from stone-related inflammation and does not by itself prove infection.
A positive nitrite points toward a urinary tract infection rather than an uncomplicated stone.
Persistently alkaline urine suggests struvite or calcium phosphate stones; acidic urine favors uric acid stones.
High specific gravity reflects the low fluid intake that predisposes to stones.
A normal white count is common in uncomplicated colic; marked leukocytosis with fever suggests infection or obstruction with pyelonephritis.
A rising creatinine with a solitary obstructing stone or bilateral obstruction is a urologic emergency.
Rises from dehydration, vomiting, and poor intake.
Low bicarbonate with alkaline urine suggests distal renal tubular acidosis, a cause of calcium phosphate stones.
Hypercalcemia should prompt evaluation for primary hyperparathyroidism, a reversible cause of recurrent stones.
Elevated uric acid supports uric acid stones, especially with gout or acidic urine.
Elevation suggests sepsis from obstructive pyelonephritis rather than uncomplicated colic.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging, to rule out ectopic pregnancy and guide imaging choice.

imaging.study: Noncontrast CT abdomen and pelvis (stone protocol)
imaging.preferred_when: Nonpregnant adults; first-line when the diagnosis is uncertain or complications are suspected

findings.text: Hyperdense calculus within the kidney or ureter
Hydronephrosis or hydroureter proximal to the stone
Stone size and location reported (for example, 6 mm at the ureterovesical junction)
Ureteral wall thickening or a rim sign at the obstructing stone
Alternative diagnosis found instead (for example, appendicitis, diverticulitis, aortic aneurysm)

imaging.preferred_when: Pregnancy, children, and patients in whom radiation should be avoided

findings.text: Echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing in the kidney
Ureteral jets absent or asymmetric on the obstructed side
No stone seen directly (ultrasound misses many ureteral stones)
Radio-opaque calculus along the expected course of the urinary tract
No stone seen (uric acid stones are radiolucent)

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

findings.text: Not used for stone detection; contrast can obscure small stones
May show a renal or urothelial mass when malignancy is suspected

imaging.study: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Pregnancy when ultrasound is nondiagnostic and further imaging is needed

findings.text: Hydronephrosis and perinephric fluid on the obstructed side
Stones themselves are poorly seen on MRI

initial.why: First-line: hematuria, pyuria, pH, and signs of infection
Assesses renal function and hydration; creatinine rise suggests significant obstruction
Looks for leukocytosis suggesting infection or obstruction with pyelonephritis
Rules out pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy before imaging

initial.test: Noncontrast CT abdomen and pelvis (stone protocol)
initial.why: Most accurate test for stone size, location, and obstruction in nonpregnant adults

initial.only_if: pregnant, child, or radiation should be avoided

supporting.why: Screens for hypercalcemia and primary hyperparathyroidism
Supports uric acid stones, especially with gout or acidic urine
Adds to the metabolic stone evaluation

supporting.only_if: fever, hypotension, or suspected obstructive pyelonephritis

supporting.why: Can follow radio-opaque stone passage when CT is not repeated
supporting.only_if: known radio-opaque stone and CT is not being repeated

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Contrast can obscure stones; noncontrast CT is the correct study

not_indicated.test: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast
not_indicated.why: Stones are poorly seen; reserve for pregnancy when ultrasound is nondiagnostic
No role in flank pain unless aortic dissection or pulmonary embolism is suspected
Not needed unless the pain is epigastric or pancreatitis is suspected
Not indicated for isolated flank pain without chest pain or cardiac symptoms

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant; ultrasound is preferred in pregnancy
Fever, chills, or hemodynamic instability with obstruction suggests infected hydronephrosis and requires urgent decompression, not just pain control
A solitary kidney, bilateral obstruction, or rising creatinine is a urologic emergency
Stone size and location guide whether to trial passage or refer for urologic intervention
Recurrent stones warrant a metabolic evaluation including calcium, uric acid, and stone analysis

differential.name: Acute pyelonephritis
differential.why_considered: Flank pain with nausea and vomiting can look identical to renal colic, and both can cause pyuria and hematuria.
differential.trigger: Fever, chills, or rigors with flank pain, or a toxic-appearing patient

history: Fever and chills preceding or accompanying the pain
Dysuria, frequency, or urgency for days
Constant rather than colicky pain
Recent urinary tract infection or instrumentation
exam: Costovertebral angle tenderness that is constant and severe
Ill-appearing, not writhing between pain waves
labs: Positive urine nitrite and leukocyte esterase with many bacteria
imaging: No obstructing stone on noncontrast CT
Perinephric fat stranding or a striated nephrogram
Hydronephrosis only if there is coexisting obstruction

differential.name: Obstructive pyelonephritis (infected hydronephrosis)
differential.why_considered: A stone that obstructs and becomes infected is the most dangerous mimic and can present with flank pain plus fever.
differential.trigger: Fever, chills, or hypotension in a patient with known or suspected stone

history: Fever and rigors with flank pain
Rapidly worsening systemic illness
Known stone or recent urologic procedure
exam: Toxic appearance, hypotension, or altered mental status
imaging: Obstructing stone with hydronephrosis on CT or ultrasound

differential.name: Acute appendicitis
differential.why_considered: Right-sided abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting can be mistaken for a stone migrating down the right ureter.
differential.trigger: Pain that migrates to and localizes in the right lower quadrant with focal tenderness

history: Periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant
Anorexia and low-grade fever
Pain worse with movement or coughing, not colicky
exam: Focal right lower quadrant tenderness with guarding
labs: Normal urinalysis or only mild pyuria
imaging: Enlarged noncompressible appendix with periappendiceal fat stranding on CT or ultrasound

differential.name: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
differential.why_considered: Sudden severe flank or back pain with hypotension in an older adult can mimic renal colic.
differential.trigger: Older adult with sudden severe flank or back pain, hypotension, or a pulsatile abdominal mass

history: Sudden onset of severe, tearing back or flank pain
Syncope or near-syncope
Known aneurysm or smoking history
imaging: Aortic aneurysm with retroperitoneal hematoma on CT angiography or bedside ultrasound

differential.name: Ovarian torsion
differential.why_considered: Sudden severe one-sided lower abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting in a female patient can mimic a stone.
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of severe pelvic pain with vomiting in a female patient

history: Sudden onset of severe pelvic pain
Vomiting at the onset
Known ovarian cyst or prior torsion
imaging: Enlarged ovary with reduced or absent Doppler flow on ultrasound

differential.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal or flank pain with nausea in a patient who could be pregnant can be mistaken for renal colic.
differential.trigger: Any patient of childbearing potential with abdominal pain

history: Missed period or abnormal vaginal bleeding
Sudden severe lower abdominal pain
Syncope or shoulder pain if ruptured
exam: Peritoneal signs and hypotension if ruptured
imaging: No intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound

differential.name: Musculoskeletal back strain
differential.why_considered: Flank and back pain are common in both, and patients may attribute stone pain to a strain.

history: Pain related to movement, lifting, or posture
No colicky waves or radiation to the groin
No nausea or vomiting
imaging: No stone or hydronephrosis if imaging is obtained

differential.name: Diverticulitis
differential.why_considered: Left lower quadrant or flank pain with fever and leukocytosis can overlap with a left ureteral stone.

history: Left lower quadrant pain with change in bowel habits
Fever and anorexia
Prior diverticulitis
labs: Normal urinalysis or only mild pyuria
imaging: Colonic diverticula with wall thickening and pericolic fat stranding on CT

differential.name: Testicular torsion
differential.why_considered: A stone at the ureterovesical junction can cause referred pain to the testicle, and torsion also causes acute severe pain.
differential.trigger: Acute testicular pain or swelling in a male patient

history: Sudden onset of severe testicular pain
Nausea and vomiting
No colicky flank pain
imaging: Reduced or absent testicular Doppler flow on ultrasound

severity.mild: Small stone (less than 5 mm) with intermittent colic, no fever, normal renal function, and able to tolerate oral fluids; likely to pass spontaneously
severity.moderate: Stone 5–10 mm with persistent severe pain, vomiting, or dehydration; may require analgesia and a trial of passage or urologic referral
severity.severe: Stone larger than 10 mm or impacted with significant hydronephrosis, uncontrolled pain, or rising creatinine; usually needs urologic intervention
severity.critical: Obstructing stone with infection (obstructive pyelonephritis), sepsis, solitary kidney, or bilateral obstruction with acute kidney injury; requires emergency decompression

red_flags.finding: Fever, chills, or rigors with flank pain
red_flags.meaning: Suggests infected hydronephrosis or pyelonephritis; needs urgent decompression and antibiotics, not just pain control
Possible sepsis from obstructive pyelonephritis or a ruptured aortic aneurysm
Bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a solitary kidney; a urologic emergency
May indicate a large or impacted stone requiring intervention

red_flags.finding: Persistent vomiting and inability to keep fluids down
red_flags.meaning: Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance; may need IV fluids and admission

red_flags.finding: Known solitary kidney or transplant kidney with obstruction
red_flags.meaning: Loss of the remaining renal function is imminent; emergency decompression

complications.name: Urinary tract infection
clues: Positive urine nitrite and leukocyte esterase

complications.name: Recurrent stone formation
clues: Low fluid intake or dietary risk factors

special_populations.differences: Flank pain may be attributed to pregnancy discomfort; physiologic hydronephrosis of pregnancy complicates imaging. Ultrasound is first-line, with MRI if needed. Urinary stasis increases infection risk, and management must consider fetal safety.

Young children may present with vague abdominal pain, vomiting, or irritability rather than classic colic. Ultrasound is preferred to avoid radiation, and underlying metabolic or anatomic causes are more likely.
Pain may be milder or blunted and confused with musculoskeletal back pain or diverticulitis. Fever may be absent even with obstruction, and renal reserve is lower.
Patients with chronic kidney disease may have less pain and are at higher risk for obstruction-related acute kidney injury. Stone burden may be larger at presentation, and contrast should be avoided.
Higher risk of infection and emphysematous pyelonephritis; may present with sepsis rather than classic colic. Glucose control affects outcomes.
Higher stone recurrence and more difficult imaging; pain may be attributed to other causes. CT image quality may be limited.

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the pain, and does it move or radiate anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Flank or costovertebral angle pain radiating down and forward to the lower abdomen, groin, or genitalia

key_questions.question: How did the pain start, and how has it changed since?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset reaching full intensity within minutes to an hour, then waxing and waning colicky waves

key_questions.question: What does the pain feel like, and how bad is it at its worst?
key_questions.looking_for: Severe cramping or colicky pain, often described as the worst pain ever, 8-10/10

key_questions.question: Does anything make it better or worse, and can you get comfortable?
key_questions.looking_for: Nothing relieves it; patient paces or writhes and cannot find a comfortable position

key_questions.question: Have you noticed blood in your urine, or any change in the color or smell?
key_questions.looking_for: Visible or microscopic hematuria; cloudy or foul-smelling urine suggests infection

key_questions.question: Have you had nausea, vomiting, or trouble keeping fluids down?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea and vomiting from the pain; persistent vomiting suggests dehydration and need for IV fluids

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, chills, or rigors?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever or chills with obstruction suggests infected hydronephrosis or pyelonephritis and needs urgent decompression

key_questions.question: Have you had a kidney stone before, or does anyone in your family have them?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior stone or family history; both are strong risk factors and raise the likelihood of recurrence

key_questions.question: How much water do you drink in a typical day?
key_questions.looking_for: Low daily fluid intake or chronic dehydration, a strong modifiable risk factor

key_questions.question: What do you eat and drink regularly, and do you take any supplements?
key_questions.looking_for: High sodium, high animal protein, high oxalate foods, excess vitamin C or vitamin D, or calcium supplements taken without food

key_questions.question: Do you take any medications, especially topiramate, acetazolamide, or diuretics?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that promote stone formation such as topiramate, acetazolamide, indinavir, or furosemide

key_questions.question: Do you have gout, diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, or have you had bariatric surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that raise stone risk or point to a specific stone type

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Excludes ectopic pregnancy and guides imaging choice; ultrasound is preferred in pregnancy

key_questions.question: Any burning with urination, urinary frequency, or urgency?
key_questions.looking_for: May occur with a stone near the ureterovesical junction, but prominent symptoms suggest urinary tract infection

key_questions.question: Any vaginal bleeding or discharge, or testicular pain or swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests a gynecologic or testicular cause such as ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, or testicular torsion

reasoning_points: Sudden severe colicky flank pain radiating to the lower abdomen, groin, or genitalia
Restlessness and inability to find a comfortable position, unlike peritoneal pain
Nausea and vomiting accompanying the pain
Hematuria on urinalysis, which is present in most but not all patients
Costovertebral angle tenderness on the affected side without peritoneal signs
Noncontrast CT showing a hyperdense calculus with hydronephrosis or hydroureter proximal to it
Pregnancy excluded before imaging in anyone who could be pregnant
Fever, chills, or hemodynamic instability excluded, since obstruction with infection is a urologic emergency
Renal function assessed, because a rising creatinine with obstruction or a solitary kidney is an emergency
Alternative diagnoses considered and excluded, including pyelonephritis, appendicitis, ruptured aortic aneurysm, ovarian torsion, and ectopic pregnancy

easy: Middle-aged adult with classic sudden severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Restless and writhing, unable to get comfortable
Noncontrast CT shows an obstructing stone with hydronephrosis
medium: Stone at the ureterovesical junction causing urinary frequency, urgency, and dysuria that mimic a urinary tract infection
Lower ureteral stone with referred pain to the testicle or labia
Woman of reproductive age with pelvic and flank pain requiring pregnancy exclusion and gynecologic look-alikes considered
Sterile pyuria from stone-related inflammation mistaken for infection
hard: Older adult with mild or blunted pain mistaken for musculoskeletal back strain or diverticulitis
Afebrile patient with obstruction who is nonetheless developing infected hydronephrosis
Pregnant patient with flank pain and physiologic hydronephrosis complicating imaging interpretation
Young child with vague abdominal pain, vomiting, or irritability rather than classic colic
Patient with a solitary kidney or bilateral obstruction presenting with rising creatinine and little pain
Uric acid stone that is radiolucent and not seen on plain x-ray
